notes.title: Notes: the neem tree
notes.text: The neem tree grows in almost every village in India. It can live in dry places where many other trees die, because its roots go deep to find water. For hundreds of years, people have used its twigs to clean their teeth. Its bitter leaves are dried and kept with grain and clothes, because insects stay away from them. Farmers also make a spray from neem seeds to protect their crops without strong chemicals. On hot afternoons, the wide shade of a neem tree is a favourite place for people to rest and talk.

titles.right: The neem tree and its uses
wrong: How to plant a tree
Insects in Indian villages

points.text: Grows in dry places: deep roots find water
Twigs used to clean teeth
Dried leaves keep insects from grain and clothes
Seed spray protects crops without strong chemicals
Leaves taste bitter
People rest and talk in the afternoon

summaries.right: The neem tree survives dry places because its roots reach deep water. People use its twigs to clean teeth, its dried leaves to keep insects from grain and clothes, and a spray from its seeds to protect crops. It also gives wide shade.
wrong: The neem tree grows in villages. People like to sit under it on hot afternoons and talk with their friends, and its leaves taste very bitter.
Farmers spray chemicals on their crops every week, so neem trees die in dry places where their roots cannot find water.

notes.title: Notes: saving rainwater
notes.text: In many Indian towns, wells run dry before the summer is over, even though the monsoon brings heavy rain. Most of that rain runs off roofs and roads into drains and is lost. Rainwater harvesting is a simple way to keep it. Pipes carry water from the roof into a tank, or into a pit filled with stones and sand that lets it soak into the ground. The stored water can be used for washing and gardens, and the water that soaks in raises the level of wells nearby. In Chennai, a rule made such systems compulsory on new buildings, and within a few years the level of water under the ground rose in many areas.

titles.right: Saving rainwater in towns
wrong: The history of the monsoon
Building new houses in Chennai

points.text: Wells dry up though the monsoon is heavy
Most rain runs off into drains and is lost
Harvesting: roof pipes lead to a tank or a soak pit
Stored water for washing and gardens; wells refill
The pit is filled with stones and sand
Chennai's rule raised underground water

summaries.right: Towns lose most monsoon rain to drains, so wells run dry. Rainwater harvesting leads roof water into tanks or soak pits; the water is used at home and refills wells. After Chennai made it compulsory, the underground water level rose.
wrong: The monsoon brings heavy rain to India every year. Roads and roofs become wet, and drains carry the water away to the sea.
Chennai built a large tank to store water for gardens, because its wells were full and the monsoon did not come that year.

notes.title: Notes: why sleep matters
notes.text: Sleep is not simply time when the body switches off. While we sleep, the brain sorts the day's experiences and stores what is important as long-term memory, which is why a night's sleep after studying helps us remember. The body also repairs muscles and grows, especially in children and teenagers, who need nine to eleven hours each night. Without enough sleep, people find it harder to concentrate, become irritable and make more mistakes. Scientists have found that the light from phone and computer screens late at night delays the feeling of sleepiness. Keeping screens away for an hour before bed, and going to sleep at the same time every night, are two of the easiest ways to sleep better.

titles.right: Why sleep matters and how to get enough
wrong: How phones are made
The best time to study for tests

points.text: Brain stores important experiences as memory
Body repairs and grows; young people need nine to eleven hours
Too little sleep: poor focus, bad temper, mistakes
Screen light at night delays sleepiness
Tips: no screens an hour before bed; a fixed bedtime
Sleep is not the body switching off

summaries.right: During sleep the brain stores memories and the body repairs and grows; the young need nine to eleven hours. Lack of sleep harms focus, mood and accuracy. Screen light delays sleep, so avoid screens before bed and keep a fixed bedtime.
wrong: Scientists study phones and computers to find out why people become irritable and make mistakes when they study at night.
Children and teenagers should study for nine to eleven hours every night, because the brain stores memories while they are awake.

notes.title: Notes: plastic in the sea
notes.text: Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic reach the oceans, carried by rivers, wind and drains. Unlike paper or food, plastic does not rot away; it breaks into smaller and smaller pieces that can last for hundreds of years. Sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, and seabirds feed bits of plastic to their chicks. The tiny pieces are also eaten by fish, so plastic can end up in the food people eat. Some countries have banned thin plastic bags, and beach clean-ups are held in many cities. The surest answer, however, is to use less plastic in the first place: carrying cloth bags and steel bottles makes a real difference.

titles.right: Plastic in the sea and what we can do
wrong: How jellyfish find food
The history of steel bottles

points.text: Rivers, wind and drains carry plastic to the sea
Plastic does not rot; it breaks into tiny pieces
Turtles, seabirds and fish eat it; it reaches our food
Some countries ban thin bags; beach clean-ups
Best answer: use less plastic
Turtles eat jellyfish

summaries.right: Plastic reaches the sea through rivers, wind and drains and breaks into tiny lasting pieces. Sea animals eat it, and it enters our food. Bans and clean-ups help, but using less plastic, with cloth bags and steel bottles, helps most.
wrong: Sea turtles and seabirds live near beaches in many cities, where people hold clean-ups and carry cloth bags.
Paper and food rot away in the sea within a few days, so plastic bags are safer for turtles and fish.

titles.right: Bridges grown from tree roots

Takes fifteen years or more to grow strong

Betel-nut trunks are hollow

summaries.right: In Meghalaya, the Khasi people guide rubber-fig roots across streams to grow bridges. A bridge takes fifteen years or more to grow, but then becomes stronger every year, unlike wood or steel. Scientists study them as building with nature.
wrong: Meghalaya has many streams and hills, and the Khasi people walk across steel bridges built by scientists every year.
Rubber-fig trees grow quickly near rivers, and their roots can carry fifty people after one rainy season.

titles.right: A garden for our school
wrong: Broken desks behind the lab
How to cook spinach

points.text: Empty space behind the lab could be a garden
A garden teaches science, maths and English
Each class looks after one bed, twenty minutes a week
Sign the paper outside the office
The space is full of weeds
The canteen could cook the spinach

summaries.right: The speaker wants to turn the empty space behind the lab into a garden that would teach science, maths and English. If each class looks after one bed for twenty minutes a week, nobody is overloaded. Listeners should sign the paper.
wrong: The speaker says the canteen should cook more spinach and asks classes to stop leaving broken desks behind the lab.
Gardens are too much work for schools, so the speaker asks thirty classes to sign a paper against the plan.

titles.right: Fireflies: how and why they glow
wrong: Street lights at night
Beetles that live in rivers

points.text: Chemicals mix with oxygen: light with almost no heat
They glow to find a partner, in coded patterns
Becoming rare: lights confuse them, homes are lost
Help: turn off outdoor lights, keep wild grass
Fields near rivers fill with lights
A bulb wastes energy as heat

summaries.right: Fireflies glow when chemicals in their tails mix with oxygen, making cold light. They flash coded patterns to find a partner. They are becoming rare because street lights confuse them, but turning off outdoor lights and keeping wild grass can help.
wrong: Fireflies are small beetles that live in warm fields near rivers, and bulbs waste energy as heat instead of light.
Street lights help fireflies find partners, so towns should keep more lights on near ponds at night.

titles.right: Plastic straws: the problem and the ban
wrong: How to recycle paper
Turtles of the Indian Ocean

points.text: Millions used briefly; they slip past recycling into the sea
Break into microplastics eaten by sea animals
Some cities ban them; cafes use other straws
Critics: a tiny part of the problem; some disabled people need them
Supporters: a first step that makes people think
Microplastics found in sea salt

summaries.right: Millions of plastic straws slip past recycling into the sea, where they break into microplastics that animals eat. Some cities ban them. Critics say straws are a tiny part of the problem and some disabled people need them; supporters call the ban a first step.
wrong: Cafes now sell bamboo straws to turtles and seabirds, so the sea is free of plastic and microplastics.
Plastic straws are useful because they bend, so every city should make more of them and recycle them.

titles.right: Testing the five-second rule
wrong: How bacteria grow
Watermelon is good for you

points.text: Scientists dropped foods on floors covered with bacteria
Bacteria moved in under one second; no safe time
Wet food picked up the most
Conclusion: the rule is a myth that does not keep us safe
Carpet passed fewer bacteria than tiles
The test was in 2016

summaries.right: Scientists dropped foods onto floors covered with bacteria and found the bacteria moved in under one second, so there is no safe time. Wet food picked up the most. The five-second rule may comfort us, but it does not keep food safe.
wrong: Carpet is the cleanest floor in a house, so food dropped on it can be eaten for up to five minutes.
Children like the five-second rule because watermelon and sweets taste better after falling on the floor.

titles.right: How much water our school wastes
wrong: How to use a stopwatch
The school garden in October

summaries.right: For a week, Class 7B checked every tap, toilet and the hose. Leaking taps, running cisterns and the hose waste about 1,500 litres a day. Repairs, a hose timer and reminders would fix cheap faults that cause most waste.
wrong: Class 7B used a stopwatch and buckets to find out how fast water flows from the garden hose every morning.
The school has forty-two taps and must buy new toilets, which will cost many lakhs of rupees.

titles.right: Switch off: saving electricity at school

wrong: The speaker went on holiday and left a tap open, so the school paid thousands of rupees for water.
One fan does not matter, so the speaker asks pupils to buy new football nets with the library's money.

titles.right: How much homework is too much
wrong: Why children should never study
Dinner time in Indian homes

points.text: Homework has grown into a second school day
It helps practice, habit and parents
Over an hour adds little and costs sleep and play
Fixes: one shared calendar, time limits, reading
Children are not machines
Copying answers at ten o'clock

summaries.right: Homework has grown into a second school day. It builds practice and habit, but for young children more than an hour adds little and costs sleep and play. Schools should share a calendar, limit homework by time and include reading, leaving children time to live.
wrong: Parents should help children copy answers at ten o'clock so that homework is finished before bedtime.
Homework should be abolished in every school because practice does not fix skills in the memory.

titles.right: How the monsoon works
wrong: The history of Kerala
Farming in the Western Ghats

points.text: Land heats faster than sea, making low pressure
Wind blows from sea to land carrying vapour
Rising air cools and the vapour falls as rain
It is irregular; El Niño can weaken it
Warming brings fewer, heavier bursts
The smell of rain on dry earth

summaries.right: The land heats faster than the sea, so wind blows inland carrying vapour, which falls as rain where the air rises and cools. The monsoon is irregular and can be weakened by El Niño, and warming is bringing fewer, heavier bursts of rain.
wrong: The monsoon starts in Kerala because the Western Ghats are cold, and it always brings the same rain every year.
Farmers smell the first rain on dry earth in June and then cool the land with water from reservoirs.

It shows people that they matter

summaries.right: The speaker argues that learning more than one language exercises the brain, shows people they matter and opens windows on new ideas. Everyone should learn at least hello, thank you and sorry in a neighbour's language.
wrong: The speaker says English opens every door, so other languages are a waste of time for children.
Amma means mother in Tamil, Kannada and Telugu, so these languages are really the same language.

summaries.right: Kamala learned the stars with her father and, as a girl, found errors in the observatory's printed tables, but the correction did not name her. She worked thirty years as a lower-paid assistant. Historians now find many such hidden workers in science.
wrong: Kamala's father was a clerk who wrote the observatory's tables in Tamil, English and Latin.
The observatory director found the mistakes in the tables himself and thanked Kamala's father.

titles.right: Why the library's evening visits grew

How to borrow a book

summaries.right: When the library opened until nine, evening visits doubled, but mainly because students came for quiet tables and free internet. The lesson: a service works when it gives people what they lack, so towns should ask residents first.
wrong: The council surveyed four hundred visitors and decided to close the library at six to save electricity.
More people read books in the evening, so every town should keep all its buildings open until nine.

summaries.right: After a cycle lane was painted on Market Road, cyclists rose from ninety to three hundred and forty a day and shop sales did not fall. Lower speeds and repaired street lights also helped; towns with paint alone saw little change.
wrong: Shopkeepers on Market Road lost customers because the cycle lane took away parking spaces.
Three towns painted cycle lanes and saw many more cyclists because their weather was cooler.

titles.right: Who the homework club really helped

summaries.right: Results rose after the homework club opened, but mostly pupils already doing well attended. Struggling pupils minded siblings or caught an early bus. Moving the club to lunch tripled their attendance. Schools should check who attends before celebrating.
wrong: The homework club failed because struggling pupils were lazy and did not want to drink tea.
Test results fell after the club opened, so the head teacher closed it and moved lessons to the bus.

titles.right: Why one solar pump failed and another worked

summaries.right: Karai's solar pump at first cut diesel use and cleared debts, but when a part failed nobody could repair it, and farmers went back to diesel. Sirumalai trained people and kept a spare-parts fund. Charities should budget for training and parts.
wrong: The solar pump in Karai was badly made, so the charity bought diesel for every family instead.
Sirumalai's pump worked better because the village is sunnier and its well is deeper.

titles.right: Why a later school start helped

Cooks at Riverside School

summaries.right: After Riverside started an hour later, late arrivals fell and marks rose, but many pupils did not sleep longer; breakfast made the difference. A school breakfast then made attendance almost perfect. Schools should measure sleep and breakfast separately.
wrong: Riverside's pupils slept an extra hour every night, which is why their marks rose in every class.
The visiting doctor said teenagers need porridge, so the school started an hour earlier to cook it.

titles.right: How the moved market succeeded
wrong: The old clock tower
Bus routes in Vellur

summaries.right: Vellur's market moved from crowded lanes to a field, and takings fell at first. The council added shade, roofs and a bus stop, and takings then rose and new stalls opened. Its willingness to watch and adjust saved the move.
wrong: Traders wanted the market moved to the field, and takings rose on the very first day.
The market stayed in the old lanes, where two cafes and a bookshop now sell vegetables.

titles.right: What made pupils read more

summaries.right: Hillcrest set aside twenty minutes of silent reading after lunch, and library borrowing almost trebled, mainly because pupils saw their teachers reading. A school whose teachers marked books instead saw no change. A school that wants readers should begin with its staff.
wrong: Hillcrest gave pupils prizes for reading after lunch, so the number of books borrowed trebled.
Teachers at Hillcrest marked exercise books while pupils read detective stories and poetry.

charts.title: Trees planted by each class
paragraph: The bar chart shows how many trees four classes planted during the school's green week.
Class 8 planted the most, with 60 trees, while Class 9 planted the fewest, only 25.
Class 6 came second with 45 trees, fifteen more than Class 7.
Overall, the four classes planted 160 trees, so the green week was a success.

charts.title: How pupils travel to school
paragraph: The chart shows how the 400 pupils of a school travel there each day.
The bus is the most common way, used by 150 pupils, and walking comes next with 120.
Only 50 pupils come by car, the smallest group.
In short, most pupils use the bus or their own feet, and very few are driven.

charts.title: Rainfall in a town, by month
paragraph: The chart gives the rainfall in a town for the four monsoon months.
Rain rose sharply from 90 millimetres in June to a peak of 210 in July.
After July it fell, to 180 in August and 120 in September.
So the monsoon was strongest in the middle of the season and weakest at its start.

charts.title: Library books borrowed, by type
paragraph: The chart compares the number of library books borrowed in one term, by type of book.
Stories were by far the most popular, with 340 borrowed, ahead of comics at 260.
Science books reached 150, while history and poetry trailed at 90 and 40.
The library might therefore buy more stories and try to make poetry more attractive.
